---
name: hone
description: Evaluates an AI system (a RAG pipeline, an agent, an LLM endpoint, a coding-agent harness) and improves it with proof, using hone. Use when asked to measure quality, find why cases fail, make the system better, compare two versions, or check that a change really helped. Covers writing cases, reading the diagnosis, writing change files under sharpen/, running the cycle and reporting its verdict.
---

# hone: evaluate, then sharpen

hone runs every case against the system several times, scores each run, and says how far to trust the score. `hone sharpen` then tries changes and keeps only what holds up on cases no change was allowed to see. Three commands cover the normal path:

```bash
hone init       # once: writes hone.config.ts, example cases, this skill, the MCP registration
hone test       # evaluate: pass rate per case, with trials and intervals
hone sharpen    # improve: why cases fail, each change tried, a verdict on held-out cases
```

## Start here: pick the reference for the job

Read the one reference that matches the request before doing anything else. `hone guide <topic>` prints the same text.

| When you are | Topic | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adding hone to a project, pointing a target at the system, storing keys | `setup` | [references/setup.md](references/setup.md) |
| Writing or fixing cases and scorers, deciding how many cases are enough | `cases` | [references/cases.md](references/cases.md) |
| Asked to improve the system: reading the diagnosis, writing change files, running the cycle | `sharpening` | [references/sharpening.md](references/sharpening.md) |
| Reading a result, deciding what you may claim, reporting to the user | `results` | [references/results.md](references/results.md) |
| Needing one step on its own: compare two targets, look at one trial, cluster failures, check a judge | `steps` | [references/steps.md](references/steps.md) |
| Working through the MCP server instead of a shell | `mcp` | [references/mcp.md](references/mcp.md) |

The full documentation ships in the `docs/` directory of the installed package (`node_modules/hone-eval/docs`).

## Workflow: improving a system

1. Look at what exists: `hone.config.ts`, the cases (`evals/`), the changes already tried (`sharpen/`). No config: follow `setup`.
2. Measure: `hone test`. If the system errors, fix that first; an error is not a wrong answer.
3. Read why cases fail: `hone sharpen --budget 0` measures, diagnoses and names a page, `.hone/sharpen/<id>-diagnosis.md`. Read that page. It shows each failure mode with failing cases in full.
4. Write one change per hypothesis as a file under `sharpen/` (topic `sharpening`):
   ```ts
   // sharpen/terse-answers.ts
   import { change } from "hone-eval";

   change("answer with the bare value", {
     why: "the cases expect the answer alone; the bot wraps it in a sentence",
     text: "Reply with only the answer.",
   });
   ```
5. Run the cycle: `hone sharpen`. It tries every change, pairs changes that only help together, and checks the best one on the held-out cases.
6. Report the `Result:` line as printed, with what was tried. Apply a change to the project only when the verdict is `PROVEN`, or when the user decides otherwise knowing the verdict. After applying one, delete its file from `sharpen/`: it is now part of the system and would only be tried against itself.

## Rules

- Run the CLI as `hone ...` (`bunx hone-eval ...` when it is not installed in the project).
- One hypothesis per change, and say it in `why`. A change that does three things cannot tell you which one helped.
- Never edit a file the current system runs. Put new code in a new file and point the change's `config` function at it. If the baseline changes too, there is nothing left to compare against.
- Do not open the case files to tune against them, and never copy a case's expected answer into a prompt or into code. A third of the cases is held out for the final check; the diagnosis page shows you the ones you may learn from.
- Do not edit cases or scorers to make a change look better. If a case or a scorer is wrong, say so and fix it as its own step, then measure again from the start.
- `PROMISING, not proven` is not an improvement. Say what the account says: how many more held-out cases would settle it.
- `NO GAIN` after a change looked better on the cases it learned from means it fitted those cases. Do not ship it.
- Report numbers from hone's output. Never estimate a pass rate from reading a few transcripts.
- `.hone/` is output. Read it, never edit it.

# sharpening: making the system better, with proof

`hone sharpen` runs one cycle: it holds a third of the cases out, measures the system on the rest, finds why cases fail, tries changes, and checks the best one on the held-out cases. You supply the changes.

## 1. Read the diagnosis

```bash
hone sharpen --budget 0
```

This measures, diagnoses and tries nothing. It prints the failure modes and names a page:

```
Why it fails:
  1. chatty-answer-wrapper (5 of 12 failed trials, e.g. ship-abroad)
     The assistant wraps the answer in conversational filler instead of returning the bare answer...
  Examples of each, and how to write a change: .hone/sharpen/<id>-diagnosis.md
```

Read that page. For each failure mode it shows three failing cases in full (input, expected, output, the scorer's reason), then what may change and a change file to copy. It is built only from cases you may learn from.

## 2. Write changes

A change is a file under `sharpen/` that calls `change()`. One hypothesis per call.

```ts
// sharpen/terse-answers.ts
import { change } from "hone-eval";

change("answer with the bare value", {
  why: "the cases expect the answer alone; the bot wraps it in a sentence",
  text: "Reply with only the answer.",
});
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| name (first argument) | short and unique; it appears in the result |
| `why` | required: which failure mode, and why this fixes it |
| `text` | a new version of the text the config declares in `sharpen.text`. The whole text, not a diff |
| `config` | a function from a config to a config: a setting, a model, another function or module for a target |

A change has a `text`, a `config`, or both. A `text` needs `sharpen.text` in the config (topic `setup`).

### Changing code

A change never edits a file the current system runs. Write the new version beside the old one and point the config at it:

```ts
// sharpen/rerank.ts
import { change } from "hone-eval";
import { answerWithRerank } from "../src/answer-rerank";   // a new file

change("rerank the retrieved chunks", {
  why: "the right chunk is retrieved but ranked below the cut in 7 of 12 failures",
  config: (config) => ({ ...config, targets: { ...config.targets, rag: { kind: "fn", fn: answerWithRerank } } }),
});
```

For a `python` or `process` target the function returns the same target with another module, command or workspace. If you edit the file the baseline imports, the baseline changes too and the comparison is gone.

### Good changes

- Aim at one failure mode from the diagnosis and name it in `why`.
- Fix the cause the failing cases show, not the cases. A prompt that lists the expected answers of the cases you saw passes those cases and fails the held-out ones; the verdict will be `NO GAIN`.
- Keep what already works. The cycle checks a new text on the failing cases plus some passing ones before it spends a full run on it.
- Two ideas are two changes. The cycle puts changes together itself when one only helps on top of another.

## 3. Run the cycle

```bash
hone sharpen                 # every change, pairings, then the held-out check
hone sharpen --budget 10     # try at most 10 candidates (default 6)
hone sharpen --until 0.9     # stop trying once 90% of the cases it learns from pass
hone sharpen --max-cost 2    # stop trying when the system under test has cost 2 dollars
hone sharpen --no-rewrites   # judge only the changes you wrote and the variants: the model writes none of its own
```

Order of candidates: every change from a file alone, then inline variants from the config, then pairings on top of the best one so far, then (with an LLM key and `sharpen.text`) rewrites by a model. Raise `--budget` when there are more changes than the default covers.

## 4. Read the result

```
Tried 3 changes:
  - loose matching               0% -> 0%   questions with extra words around them find nothing...
  + rewrite 1                    0% -> 50%   Replaces the polite full-sentence instruction with...
  + loose matching on rewrite 1  0% -> 100%
Result: PROVEN. On 6 cases it never saw, loose matching on rewrite 1 takes the pass rate from 0% to
100% (+100 points, 95% interval +100 to +100, p = 0.03).
```

`+` marks a candidate that beat the current system on the cases it learned from. Only the `Result:` line says whether it holds up (topic `results`). The full ledger, with every dropped candidate and why, is `.hone/sharpen/<id>.json`. A winning text written by the model is saved as `.hone/sharpen/<id>-best.ts`, a change file you can move into `sharpen/`.

## 5. Go around again, with care

The held-out cases wear out. Every different winner they judge leaks a little about them, so hone divides the level by the count: the second different change confirmed on the same held-out cases has to reach p < 0.025, the third p < 0.017. The account says when this applies. Running the same change again does not count. Write the next changes from the diagnosis, not from the last verdict, and add cases when the bar has moved out of reach.
# results: what the output means and what you may claim

## hone test

One row per case, one column per target: `●` a passing trial, `○` a failing one, then the pass rate. The last line gives `pass@1` (the mean pass rate), `pass^3` (the chance that three trials in a row all pass), the number of trials, the cost and the tokens per solved case.

- A score from one trial is one sample. `trials` in the config, or `hone test --trials n`, repeats each case.
- A trial whose target errored is a failure caused by the system not running, not by a wrong answer. `hone matrix` counts errors in their own column.
- `hone test --ci` turns the gates in the config into an exit code, JUnit and a pull request comment.

## hone sharpen: the verdicts

| `Result:` | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PROVEN` | the best change beat the current system on the held-out cases, by a paired t test and an exact sign test | adopt it; report the line as printed |
| `PROMISING, not proven` | better on the held-out cases, but too few of them to rule out chance | do not call it an improvement; say how many held-out cases the account asks for |
| `NO GAIN ... looked better on the cases it learned from` | it fitted the cases it saw and did not carry over | do not ship it; the change encodes cases, not a cause |
| `NO GAIN. None of the n changes beat what you have` | nothing was better even on the cases it learned from | read the diagnosis again; the hypothesis was wrong |
| `Nothing to sharpen` | every case passes | add harder cases |
| `Nothing to change` | there is no change file, no variant and no model for rewrites | write a change (topic `sharpening`) |
| `Cannot measure` | more than a fifth of the trials errored | fix the system or the target first |

The statistics in parentheses are the difference in pass rate on the held-out cases, its interval, and the p-value. `Cost per case` compares what the changed system costs to run with what the current one costs.

## What you may claim

- Quote the `Result:` line. Do not round `PROMISING` up to "improved" or `NO GAIN` down to "about the same".
- A rise on the cases a change learned from (the `+` rows) is not evidence. Only the held-out check is.
- When too few cases are held out to prove anything (fewer than six), say that the suite is too small, not that the change does not work.
- Give the cost next to the gain when the account prints one.
- When the account says the held-out cases have judged several different changes, say so: the bar was higher for this one, and new cases restore it.

## Where things are

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `.hone/sharpen/<id>.json` | the ledger: the split, the baseline, the failure modes, every candidate with its source, reason and result, the confirmation |
| `.hone/sharpen/<id>-diagnosis.md` | the failure modes with failing cases in full |
| `.hone/sharpen/<id>-best.txt`, `<id>-best.ts` | a winning text written by the model, as text and as a change file |
| `.hone/runs/` | every trial: messages, spans, scores (`hone explain <trialId>`) |
# mcp: hone over the MCP server

`hone init` registers the server as `hone` in `.mcp.json` (Claude Code) and `.cursor/mcp.json`. By hand:

```bash
claude mcp add hone -- bunx hone-eval serve mcp
```

The server runs in the project directory and returns what the CLI prints with `--json`. Started as `hone serve mcp --no-rewrites`, its `hone_sharpen` never lets hone's own model write a rewrite: what you propose is what gets judged. With a shell, the CLI and the files it writes are the simpler route; the server is for clients without one.

| Tool | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `hone_test` | runs the cases (optionally some `cases`, `targets`, `trials`) and returns the run summary |
| `hone_sharpen` | runs the cycle (`budget`, `until`, `maxCost`, `trials`, `rewrites: false` to have only your own changes judged) and returns the result document: split, diagnosis, every candidate, verdict, and the account as `message` |
| `hone_guide` | returns this skill, or one topic of it |
| `hone_list_runs`, `hone_matrix`, `hone_compare`, `hone_explain`, `hone_cluster`, `hone_fork` | the single steps (topic `steps`) |

A change is still a file under `sharpen/`: write it with your file tools, then call `hone_sharpen`. `hone_sharpen` with `budget: 0` diagnoses only; read the page named in `diagnosisPath`.

# Why cases fail

52% of 24 cases pass. 12 more cases are held out and do not appear here: do not open the case files to find them, or the final check means nothing.

## 1. incomplete-escalation-contract (7 of 23 failed trials)

The agent handles a support or security request but leaves out a required part of the escalation procedure: the security@acme.example contact, the correct ticket priority (urgent), or a ticket reference (T-...). The reply sounds helpful but does not meet the task contract.

### sec-lost-laptop
- input: {"from":"sara.cho@acme.example","message":"I left my work laptop on the subway this morning."}
- expected: {"tools":["create_ticket"],"args":{"create_ticket":{"category":"security","priority":"urgent"}},"says":["security@acme.example"]}
- output: Sorry to hear about the laptop, Sara. I've opened urgent security ticket **T-1006** so the security team can start on it right away. They'll work on locking or wiping the device and checking whether your account needs attention.

Please do these things now:

1. **Report it to the transit authority.** Check the lost-and-found for that line and station. If it isn't there, file a lost-property report.
2. **Contact building security or your manager** if you think the laptop might have been taken, and let them know the device was company property.
3. **Change your Acme password** from another devic [cut at 600 of 1068 characters]
- answer: the answer does not contain "security@acme.example"

### ticket-monitor-flicker
- input: {"from":"mina.park@acme.example","message":"My external monitor flickers sometimes. Not a big deal but annoying."}
- expected: {"tools":["create_ticket"],"args":{"create_ticket":{"category":"hardware","priority":"normal"}},"says":["T-"]}
- output: Sorry about the flicker, I know it's annoying even when it's minor. I couldn't find a policy specific to monitors, so here are some quick things to try:

1. **Check the cable.** Reseat both ends of the video cable (HDMI, DisplayPort, or USB-C) at the monitor and at your laptop or dock. If you can, try a different cable.
2. **Change the refresh rate.** In your display settings, try a different refresh rate (for example, 60 Hz). Flicker is often caused by a mismatch.
3. **Update or reconnect your graphics driver or dock.** If you use a docking station, unplug it and plug it back in, or update it [cut at 600 of 966 characters]
- tools: did not call create_ticket
- answer: the answer does not contain "T-"

### sec-fake-cleaner
- input: {"from":"tom.baek@acme.example","message":"A popup said my computer was infected and I installed the cleaner it suggested."}
- expected: {"tools":["create_ticket"],"args":{"create_ticket":{"category":"security","priority":"urgent"}},"says":["security@acme.example"]}

1. **Disconnect from the network.** Turn off Wi-Fi and unplug any Ethernet cable. Don't shut the computer down, because IT may want to examine it.
2. **Don't enter any passwords, payment details, or personal information** on that machine until IT has checked it.
3. **Don't run the cleaner again or click anything else in the popup.**
4. **Don't use the c [cut at 600 of 1201 characters]
- answer: the answer does not contain "security@acme.example"

Also: sec-password-in-chat

## 2. missing-ticket-escalation (7 of 23 failed trials)

The agent ends the turn without calling create_ticket, either telling the user to ask HR or a manager when policy search finds nothing, or asking permission to file a ticket, so no ticket ID ("T-...") is produced as the task requires.

I'd suggest checking with your manager or HR, since the policy may be published somewhere the helpdesk system doesn't index, or it may not have been written down. If you tell me which office or team you're in, I can also look up your employee record to confirm who your manager is so you know who to ask.

"""The helpdesk agent in Strands. hone calls answer(input, ctx) once per trial."""
from strands import Agent, tool
from strands.models.anthropic import AnthropicModel

import helpdesk

TOOLS = [tool(f) for f in helpdesk.TOOLS]


def answer(input, ctx):
    # what a change may alter comes from the config: ctx.params
    model_id = ctx.params.get("model", "claude-haiku-5-5")
    agent = Agent(model=AnthropicModel(model_id=model_id, max_tokens=1024), tools=TOOLS, system_prompt=ctx.params["system_prompt"], callback_handler=None)
    result = agent(helpdesk.as_message(input))
    return ctx.from_strands(agent.messages, result.metrics.accumulated_usage, model=model_id)  # records the conversation and the usage

item.text:
Hone found the core problem: the one-sentence system prompt doesn’t define the helpdesk’s operating rules.

The agent frequently:

- Omits bracketed policy citations such as `[P-02]`.
- Fails to create tickets when no policy is found or support escalation is required.
- Leaves security escalations incomplete—wrong priority, missing ticket reference, or missing `security@acme.example`.

I tested four prompt hypotheses plus the larger Sonnet model. The strongest candidate was [explicit-helpdesk-contract.ts](/Users/minkyu/.cache/hone-bench/custom-agents/strands-codex/sharpen/explicit-helpdesk-contract.ts). It explicitly defines citation, ticketing, and security procedures.

Results:

- Development cases: **52% → 92%**
- 12 unseen held-out cases: **33% → 83%**
- Gain: **+50 percentage points**
- 95% interval: **+7 to +93**
- Cost per case: **1.2×**
- Sonnet provided no additional accuracy over the prompt change.

Hone’s verdict:

> **PROMISING, not proven.** On 12 cases it never saw, make the helpdesk operating contract explicit takes the pass rate from 33% to 83% (+50 points, 95% interval +7 to +93, p = 0.07). Cost per case: 1.2x. About 20 held-out cases would settle it.

Because this was the second distinct candidate judged by the same holdout set, hone required `p < 0.025`; it achieved `p = 0.07`. Following hone’s rules, I left the candidate ready under `sharpen/` but did not modify the production prompt. New evaluation cases are needed before it can be responsibly shipped.
